description: We are a team of passionate coders and problem-solvers with diverse skills in AI/ML, AI agents, frontend, backend, full-stack development, and data analysis. For NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, we aim to combine our strengths to build robust AI-powered solutions, intelligent agents, and user-friendly applications that turn creative ideas into impactful solutions for real-world challenges.
summary: Brahmaputra Flood related to recent Assam Flood 2026 is an open-source interactive web app that uses L-band radar from the NASA-ISRO NISAR mission to show how the 2026 monsoon flood spread and drained across the Brahmaputra floodplain in Assam, India, around Kaziranga, Majuli and Morigaon/Nagaon. Monsoon clouds hide floods from optical satellites, but NISAR's radar sees through them, day and night. We mapped open water on 10 NISAR passes from 25 June to 23 October 2026 using HH backscatter. Users can play a timeline animation, swipe between any two dates, view change and flood-frequency maps, compare false-colour radar with optical imagery, and follow a flooded-area chart. The data show 1,076 km² of open water in late June, 780 to 940 km² through mid-September, then a 65% drop to 378 km² by 23 October as the monsoon withdrew. Of the 1,391 km² flooded at least once, 1,138 km² was seasonal floodplain rather than river channel. The app turns complex radar data into maps and numbers that disaster managers, park staff, farmers, students and the public can understand without SAR expertise.
details:
What it does. Brahmaputra Flood related to Assam recnent flood 2026 maps monsoon flood inundation on the Brahmaputra floodplain in central Assam, India (lon 93.0 to 94.6 E, lat 26.3 to 27.2 N), covering Kaziranga National Park, Majuli river island and the Morigaon and Nagaon districts, from 25 June to 23 October 2026. The river floods this area almost every year, and monsoon clouds blind optical satellites exactly when it matters. The app offers a timeline animation of open water across 10 NISAR passes, a before/after swipe between any two dates, a change map (newly flooded, receded, water on both dates against the first pass), a flood-frequency map, false-colour radar (R=HH, G=HV, B=HH/HV) and raw HH backscatter, optical or street basemaps with opacity control, a flooded-area chart, and plain-language notes on drivers and limits.

Data and method. We used NISAR L-band Level-2 GCOV (geocoded, terrain-corrected gamma-naught) products from the NASA ASF DAAC: track 163, descending, frame 75, HH and HV on frequency A at 10 m posting, 12-day repeat (collections NISAR_L2_GCOV_PROVISIONAL_V1 for the first nine dates and NISAR_L2_GCOV_V1 for 23 Oct). There is no pass between 19 Jul and 12 Aug because of NISAR's planned data gap. We kept one track and frame so geometry matches on every date, streamed only the study-area pixels from each roughly 7 GB file, removed values below -30 dB from sub-swath gaps, multilooked 11x11 to about 110 m, and resampled to a lat/lon grid. Water is HH below -17.25 dB, one threshold for all dates set at the valley between the water and land histogram peaks, cleaned with a 3x3 majority filter. Smooth open water reflects the radar away from the satellite, so it appears dark.

What we found. Across 15,255 km² imaged on all 10 passes, open water peaked at 1,076 km² on 25 June 2026, held at about 780 to 940 km² from July to mid-September, then fell to 378 km² by 23 October, 65% below late June. In total 1,391 km² was flooded at least once: 1,138 km² was seasonal-only floodplain and 254 km² was water on every pass, mostly the main river channel. By 23 October, 708 km² of the late-June water had drained.

Why it happens. Monsoon rain over the eastern Himalaya and Assam, plus upstream snow and glacier melt, swells the Brahmaputra and its tributaries. The low, flat, silt-raised floodplain lets water spill into fields, beels (wetlands) and Kaziranga's grasslands. Repeated rain pulses keep it wet through August, and the river drains as the monsoon withdraws in late September and October. The flood refills wetlands and fertilises farmland, but it also damages homes, roads and wildlife habitat.

Limits. Flooded vegetation (which turns bright from double-bounce scattering) and wind-roughened water can be missed, while smooth sand bars and radar shadow can be falsely flagged as water. The record starts on 25 June, the first public NISAR data, so earlier June floods are not captured. These are estimates, not official flood statistics.

Tools and technologies. Python pipeline with asf_search, h5py, fsspec, aiohttp, requests, NumPy, pyproj and Pillow. Static web app in HTML and JavaScript with Leaflet 1.9.4 and Chart.js 4.4.1, hosted on GitHub Pages, MIT licence. Basemaps: Esri World Imagery and OpenStreetMap. Source code: https://github.com/MahaveerPandey8290/brahmaputra-flood-waltz

Who it helps. Disaster managers can see where water is spreading even under cloud, Kaziranga park staff can track flooding of wildlife habitat, farmers and planners can tell land that floods every season from land that floods rarely, and students and the public get an easy picture of how radar sees floods.

Future NISAR applications. Near-real-time flood alerts every 12 days (6 days with both orbit directions), crop and wetland monitoring with HV, riverbank erosion tracking, and S-band versus L-band comparison using ISRO's Bhoonidhi S-SAR products.
